scope: Independent source, mathematics, written pedagogy, actual coordinate models, and focused rendered-DOM review of all eleven cards for main exercises 310–319, including both printed parts of 311. Every condition, prompt, explanation, justification, help item, answer contract, model note, focus label, and model state was read. This report does not replace responsive browser or actual-image review.

source.inspection: The supplied original page image was visually read before independent derivation and before reading the authored cards.

cards.verification: Source dimensions 25, 25, 40 and 8 are preserved. The base median is justified as an altitude; its length is 15. The three-perpendicular theorem gives the face altitude 17. The two right faces have area 100 each and the remaining face 340, giving lateral area 540 cm² without adding the base.

Source sides 13, 14, 15 and perpendicular edge 9 are preserved. Heron's formula gives base area 84; the base altitude is 12 with its foot inside BC, at distances 9 and 5. The other face altitude is 15; the complete four-face area is 315 cm². Targeted re-review confirms that the shortened Heron computation and verbal theorem state the same product and positive square root; all other card fields are deeply identical to the previously reviewed content.

The independently constructed orthogonal foot lies inside DE, at DH/DE=9/25. The named planes and ET parallel to AD establish BC perpendicular to DAE; HJ in DBC provides the second intersecting face direction, so AH is perpendicular to the whole face plane. Area equality gives AH=36/5 cm. The proof is assessed manually.

The synthetic derivation uses an arbitrary finite integer n≥3, the circumradius R, inradius r, and common height h. It distinguishes the edge angle from the acute face/base dihedral, proves r/R=cos(180°/n), and obtains tan α=cos(180°/n)·tan φ for 0°<φ<90°. The hexagon with R=4 and h=3 is explicitly only an illustration.

The parallel corresponding radii and named axial section justify the projection and right triangle. The difference of inradii is √3, vertical height 1, and the true face apothem 2. The three trapezoids total 54 dm². Exact coordinates preserve the notably shallow source proportions. The larger filled axial trapezoid CEFC₁ is independently recovered from all frustum edges; the inner EHF remains explicitly drawn and correctly described.

The axial section separates the vertical height 63 from the apothem 65. The half-side difference is 16; together with the 7:3 ratio this gives larger side 56 and smaller side 24 cm. Both values are verified against the original constraints, and the pair plus reasoning is assessed manually.

The midpoint square and two homotheties produce two parallel equal squares of face centroids. Joining edges are perpendicular to their planes and have length ST/3=a√2/3, equal to a square side. The resulting convex straight prism is a cube. All eight actual centroids, six supporting square faces, and twelve displayed edges are independently verified.

A shared-edge midpoint and the same one-third homothety prove the six centre distances are all a/3. The three-centre plane is parallel and distinct from the opposite original face, placing the fourth centre outside it. The four noncoplanar centres form a regular tetrahedron; hull faces and volume ratio 1/27 independently confirm this.

The four side-face centres form a square in the middle section; the other two lie on its perpendicular centre axis. All twelve prospective edges have length a√2/2. The proof establishes the eight supporting triangular faces, excludes every other possible face via opposite pairs, and checks four edges at each vertex. The full centroid hull and displayed edge graph agree.

Cutting all four corners at edge midpoints leaves a convex octahedron with exactly eight equal equilateral faces. The corner tetrahedron is similar to the original. A normal section through the midpoint K of EF gives the inward rays KA, KG and KH, with KA and KH opposite. Thus the interior angles are supplementary; independent outward-normal checks give cosines 1/3 and −1/3.

Each of the three planes through A and another vertex is the perpendicular bisector plane of the remaining edge and preserves every vertex and the convex body. Any reflection fixing A must fix exactly one of the other vertices and swap the remaining pair; the perpendicular bisector plane is unique. This proves exactly three. Every actual reflected vertex and the exhaustive 24-permutation classification agree.
